title: Max-Min Diversification with Asymmetric Distances

problem.claim: The Asymmetric Max-Min Diversification problem selects k vertices from a complete directed graph with nonnegative edge distances satisfying the directed triangle inequality to maximize the smallest pairwise distance.

gap.claim: It was unclear how to design good approximation algorithms for AMMD because the greedy strategy that gives a simple 1/2-approximation for symmetric MMD fails for AMMD.

contributions.claim: The paper initiates the study of the Asymmetric Max-Min Diversification problem.
The paper specifies AMMD on complete directed graphs with directed-triangle-inequality distances and a max-min selection objective.
The paper identifies query result diversification, web search, and facility location as natural applications of AMMD.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly distinguish their work as initiating the study of AMMD.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the greedy next-furthest-point strategy fails for AMMD.

narrative_sequence.summary: MMD is presented as a well-known and extensively studied diversity-maximization model.
The paper introduces the asymmetric variant AMMD.
AMMD is defined over a complete digraph with directed-triangle-inequality distances and a max-min objective.
The asymmetric problem generalizes symmetric MMD and has applications in diversification, search, and facility location.
The standard greedy approximation approach fails for AMMD, leaving good approximation algorithms unclear.

source_observation.claim: An asymmetric distance structure can invalidate a greedy strategy that works for the corresponding symmetric problem.

interpretation.claim: Algorithmic guarantees may depend critically on symmetry assumptions rather than only on triangle inequalities.

application.claim: When adapting diversification methods to directed or asymmetric settings, recheck the approximation argument instead of transferring the symmetric guarantee.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which alternative algorithms or guarantees succeed for AMMD.

unknowns: The abstract does not state the paper's approximation algorithms or guarantees.
The abstract does not report experiments, datasets, or quantitative evaluation.
The abstract does not provide theoretical proof details or complexity results.
